title: Guitar lessons, dancing class and the boyhood string band
summary: A failed guitar start at nine, ragtime at a neighbourhood dancing class, then a youth string band that played Carnival suppers by about 1912.

bands.name: Six and Seven Eight String Band

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Well, of course it didn't enter into anything at all. And when the marching parades happened, funeral parades, Negro processions happened to pass, they'd always come out and look at it, and listen with enjoyment, but with a tongue-in-cheek attitude towards it. My next real introduction to music, if you will, I had a grandmother who sang and played very well. My father, she sang and played the piano and accompanied herself. And my father played the guitar a little bit. He also played an alto horn. But when I was nine years old, my grandmother decided that I should play a guitar and bought me one. And they hired a very lovely lady, I remember her name, Miss Casnavette, to give me lessons. And after three lessons, she told my family I was perfectly hopeless. It was no use to persist. I was wasting their money and her time. So the guitar got put aside for about two, three years. And then the neighborhood where we lived, there was the Greenmire family, the Hanes, the Downwinds, the Frelson Pages, Esperberto, and several fellas right nearby. The mothers got together and decided that we should have a neighborhood dancing class. And I had to have a terrible spanking to make me go to the thing. I had no idea of having anything to do with girls at all. But once I got there, first thing I ran into was a trio, a piano, drums, and a bass fiddle, who now I know were playing ragtime, because I still remember the tune. It was a lizard on the rail. They call it his Hiawatha, Red Wing. And from then on, they had no trouble making me go to dancing school. But I didn't dance a doggone bit. I'd just sit around and listen to the music until the teacher made me come up and do one or two steps with her. And from then on, if there happened to be a band with a guitar in it, I would always hang around watching the musician playing it and then go home and try. Then we had a group of fellas about my age, maybe 12, that finally discovered that secretly we were each trying to play string instruments. So we finally got together and began practicing every Sunday afternoon at the home of Mr. and Ms. Robert Reynolds on Marengo in Pretania. And we finally got proficient enough until we'd call on different girls on Sunday afternoon, the whole band, which was seven or eight of us. And for sandwiches and Cokes, we'd play a whole evening. And that part was quite acceptable to everybody concerned because it was not loud music. It was all strings, violins, sometimes two violins, banjo, two guitars, bass fiddle, and a mandolin.
Well, what type of music did you end up playing? The popular music of the day or...?

Yes, but it was jazzed up. I have some examples of that. You see, of that group, which was originally seven men, four of us still play together. And a band that was at that time in its infancy became known as the six and seven eight string band. It was, became very popular and we even played for the Queen of the Carnival's Supper dance at the Stratford Club Mardi Gras Night. We had gone up to twelve. We could bring in some ringers and increase the band up that much.
And what year was that that you played?
Mm-hmm. I wasn't any more than fifteen years old then. And that was definitely...
